summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe permanent colour service: understand colour theory and the level and tone system, consult with the client and do the skin and strand tests, choose the shade and developer, mix and apply the colour for a first-time lightening, a regrowth retouch or a darker colour, process, rinse and finish, and give aftercare. It also covers grey hair, relaxed and natural hair, colour faults, safety, clean-up and records.

blocks.p: Permanent colour is the most popular chemical service in many Jamaican salons, and one of the easiest to get wrong. A client leaves with the colour she wanted, or with orange hair, stained skin, a burnt scalp or hair that breaks. This unit covers the whole service, from the first conversation to the record card. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

Colour is part science and part careful judgement. You need to understand **level** (how light or dark) and **tone** (how warm or cool), what the developer and the alkali do inside the hair, and how the hair's own colour will show when you lighten it. Then you apply the colour in the right order so that it develops evenly.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon: skin and strand tests with colour swatches, and a permanent colour regrowth or full-head application on a model or a human-hair practice head. The assessor watches your consultation, tests, mixing, application, timing, safety, clean-up and records, not only the finished colour.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, your swatches and the work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Colour and developer can stain and burn the skin, sting the eyes, cause allergy and give off fumes. Allergy to hair colour can be serious, and once a person is allergic she stays allergic. The rules below stop almost every accident.

blocks.h: Hazards and how you prevent them

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Colour or developer on your skin
Dermatitis; allergy that can last for life
Wear gloves for the whole service, including rinsing and shampooing
Wear an apron
Dry your hands and use hand cream; report sore skin early
Colour on the client's skin
Stains; irritation; burns
Barrier cream round the hairline, ears and nape
Cotton wool or a neck strip at the hairline
Cape and towel to protect clothes
Apply carefully; remove stains at the end with a skin stain remover
Colour or developer in the eyes
Pain, burns, damage to sight
Keep a dry towel in the client's hand to dab her face
Never lean the client back with colour in her hair
Rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean water if it splashes, and get medical help
Fumes (ammonia and others)
Headache, coughing, feeling sick
Work in a well-ventilated room
Keep lids on tubes, bottles and bowls
Offer fresh air to a client who feels unwell
Mixing mistakes
Wrong colour; harm to hair and skin
Use colour and developer from the same maker
Measure carefully as the maker says
Mix just before use; never store mixed colour
Metal bowls and brushes
Metal can react with the chemicals and spoil the result
Use clean plastic or glass bowls and tint brushes
Spills and wet floors
Slips; stained floors and clothes
Wipe up at once; put out a wet floor sign

blocks.note: If colour or developer gets into the client's eye, rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean, cool running water, tilting her head so the water runs away from the other eye. Keep rinsing for at least 10 to 15 minutes, do not let her rub it, and get medical help. Tell your instructor and write it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: If the client says her scalp is burning, itching or stinging during processing, **stop**. Rinse the colour off at once with lukewarm water, tell the instructor, and do not carry on. Never tell a client that burning is normal.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Keep colour tubes and developer closed, labelled, in a **cool, dry place out of direct sunlight**. Hydrogen peroxide breaks down with heat and light and loses strength. Jamaica's heat makes this a real risk.
Never pour products into unlabelled or food bottles.
Read the label, the maker's instructions and the safety data sheet (the sheet that gives hazards and first aid).

**Mix only what you need, just before use.** Mixed colour is a live chemical: do not store it, do not put it back into a tube, and do not keep it for the next client. Throw it away as the maker and the Centre say.
Never mix products from different makers, or mix colour with bleach or cleaning chemicals.
Use the oldest stock first; check the date.

blocks.note: Wear gloves and wash your hands before and after every client. Keep your nails short and smooth, so you do not scratch the scalp.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Colour theory: level, tone and the colour wheel

blocks.p: Hair colour is measured on a scale of **levels**, usually 1 to 10. Level 1 is black and level 10 is the lightest blonde. Makers use the same idea of levels, though the exact names differ a little.

head: Level
Name (typical)
rows: Black
Darkest brown
Dark brown
Medium brown
Light brown
Dark blonde
Medium blonde
Light blonde
Very light blonde
Lightest (pale) blonde

blocks.p: Most Jamaican clients have natural hair at **level 1 to 4**. Going to a blonde from there takes several levels of lift and often bleach, which is a bigger and riskier job than most clients expect.

**Tone** (or shade) is the colour you see: warm (gold, copper, red), cool (ash, blue, violet, green-based) or neutral. A colour has both a level and a tone, written on the maker's chart, for example '6.0' (level 6, natural) or '6.4' (level 6, copper).

head: Tone
Looks like
Used for
rows: Warm (gold, copper, red)
Golden, bronze, red
A rich, bright or warm look
Cool (ash, blue, violet)
Silvery, smoky; less warmth
Cancelling brassy or orange tones
Neutral (natural)
A true brown or blonde with no strong tone
A natural look; grey cover

ul: The **primary colours** are **red, yellow and blue**. They cannot be made by mixing others.
The **secondary colours** are made by mixing two primaries: **orange** (red + yellow), **green** (yellow + blue), **violet** (red + blue).
**Tertiary colours** are made by mixing a primary and a secondary.
Colours that face each other on the wheel **cancel each other out**. This is the key to correcting unwanted tones.

head: Unwanted tone
What cancels it
In the salon
rows: Yellow (brassy blonde)
Violet
A violet or blue-violet toner or an ash shade
Orange (brassy brown)
Blue
An ash (blue-based) shade
Red
Green
A matt (green-based) shade
Green
Red
A warm or red shade

blocks.note: Cancelling a tone makes it neutral, not a different colour. To neutralise orange, add blue to the mix; it will not turn her hair blue if you use the right amount.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Underlying pigment: what shows when you lighten

blocks.p: Natural hair holds the pigment **melanin**. As you lift (lighten) dark hair, the dark pigment breaks down and the warm pigments underneath are uncovered, one after another.

flow: Black or very dark brown
Red
Red-orange
Orange
Gold
Yellow
Pale yellow

ul: The darker the starting hair, the more red and orange it shows when lightened, and the harder it is to get a clean blonde.
That is why a client at level 3 who asks for a light, ash blonde needs bleach, several sessions and a toner, and still may end up with some warmth.
A good stylist tells the client honestly what is possible.

blocks.note: Colour does not lift colour. Permanent colour can darken or change the tone of hair that already has colour on it, but it cannot make it lighter. To go lighter than coloured hair, you need a lightener, and that needs an instructor's decision.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Colour and developer are mixed just before use
The alkali (often ammonia) swells the hair and opens the cuticle
Small colour molecules and the developer pass into the cortex
The developer (hydrogen peroxide) lightens some of the natural melanin
The developer makes the small colour molecules join into large ones
The large molecules are too big to wash back out, so the colour stays

ul: The **cortex** is the middle layer of the hair, where the colour is trapped.
The **alkali** (a base such as ammonia or a substitute) lifts the cuticle so that the colour can get in. It also helps the developer work.
The **developer** is hydrogen peroxide in a cream or liquid. It does two jobs: it lightens the natural pigment, and it joins the colour molecules together.
This is **oxidative** colour: it needs developer to develop. That is why the mix must be used straight after mixing.

blocks.p: Because the colour is locked inside, it does not wash out. The hair that grows from the scalp has its natural colour, so a client needs a **regrowth retouch** when new growth shows. Colour stays on the lengths until the hair is cut.

head: Type
How it works
Lasts
Lift
rows: Temporary (rinse, spray, mousse)
Coats the outside of the hair; no developer.
Until the next shampoo
None
Semi-permanent
Small molecules go partly into the hair; no developer or a very little.
About 4 to 8 shampoos
None; adds tone and shine; does not cover grey fully
Demi-permanent (deposit only)
Low alkali, low-strength developer.
Several weeks
Little or none; good for refreshing and tone; covers some grey
Permanent (oxidative)
Alkali, developer and colour molecules join inside the cortex.
Until it is grown out or cut
Can lift up to about 3 levels or so, depending on developer; best grey cover
Lightener (bleach)
Strongly removes natural pigment.
Permanent
Many levels; very harsh; needs a toner and expert care

blocks.note: Lift figures vary by maker and by hair. Use the maker's chart and your instructor's advice, not a guess.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Developer strength is named by **volume** or by **percentage** of hydrogen peroxide. Makers' names differ, so check the label.

head: Volume
Percentage
What it does (general)
rows: 10 volume
About 3%
Deposit only; a tone-on-tone result, no or very little lift; gentlest
20 volume
About 6%
Usual strength for covering grey and for about 1 to 2 levels of lift
30 volume
About 9%
More lift, about 2 to 3 levels; harsher on the hair and scalp
40 volume
About 12%
The most lift; very harsh; mostly used with lightener, not on the scalp; only on an instructor's decision

ul: **Higher strength** lifts more but is harsher on hair and scalp. **Lower strength** is gentler and lifts less.
The right developer depends on the starting level, the target level, the amount of grey and the condition of the hair.
Follow the maker's chart for strength and mixing ratio. Use the same maker's developer, and measure carefully. Wrong amounts change the result and the timing.

blocks.p: Do the consultation at the chair, with the hair dry and in good light (daylight if you can). You are deciding whether the colour can go ahead, which colour and strength to use, and what the honest result will be.

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask what colour she wants; use the shade chart and pictures
Ask about past services, allergies and health
Look at the scalp
Find the natural level, the grey and the hair's condition
Do the skin test and strand test
Choose the colour and developer
Explain the plan, time and price; agree and record

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The colour she wants and how she wears her hair
Show pictures. Be honest about what is possible from her starting level.
Past colour, bleach, relaxer, perm or smoothing treatment, and when
Treated hair is porous and fragile. Colour does not lift colour.
Henna, or home or box dye, or gradual colour restorers
Some contain metals or plant dye that can react badly with developer and damage the hair.
Allergies, past reactions to colour, sensitive skin, asthma, medicines
A past reaction to colour means no colour and a doctor's advice.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding
Follow the maker's advice; ask her to check with her doctor.
How she looks after her hair, and how often she can come for a retouch
Colour needs care and regular retouches.

blocks.h: Checking the scalp and finding the base

ul: Part the hair in several places. Look for cuts, sores, scabs, rashes, redness, or infection.
Find the natural level by comparing the **dry roots** (new growth, not the ends) with the maker's shade chart in daylight.
Look at the amount of **grey** (white) hair: a little, about half, or most. Grey hair has no pigment and its cuticle is often tight, so colour takes longer to go in.
Check porosity, elasticity, texture and density. Hair that is porous or fragile needs gentler products.

head: Finding
What you do
rows: A positive skin test (redness, swelling, itching, blisters)
Do not colour. Record it and refer her to a doctor.
Cuts, sores, scabs or rashes on the scalp
Do not colour. Wait until the scalp has healed.
A contagious scalp condition (lice, ringworm, impetigo)
Do not colour. Refer her privately and kindly; disinfect what she touched.
A past allergic reaction to hair colour
Do not colour unless a doctor agrees.
Metallic salts or unknown products on the hair (compound henna, restorers)
Do the strand test with great care, or do not colour. The hair can heat up, change colour or break.
Very weak, brittle or badly damaged hair
Do not colour. Advise treatment and a trim.
A relaxer or perm very recently
Wait the time the maker advises (often at least 2 weeks); scalp and hair need to recover.
Hair has been bleached very recently and is fragile
Take advice from your instructor before colouring.

blocks.note: A client who has coloured before without a problem can still develop an allergy later. Do a skin test before every colour service, not just the first.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Follow the maker's instructions. The usual method: clean a small patch of skin behind the ear or inside the elbow, apply a little mixed product (or the product the maker supplies) and let it dry.
Leave it uncovered and do not wash it for the time the maker says. Tell the client to wash it off and call you if it itches, burns or swells.
Do it about **48 hours** before the service, or as the maker says.
Read the result at the time the maker says. Redness, swelling, itching or blisters mean a reaction. **Do not colour.** Record it and advise her to see a doctor.
Write the date and result on the record card.

blocks.p: A strand test checks the **result and timing** of the colour on a small piece of the client's own hair, before you do the whole head.

flow: Take a small strand at the back, from a hidden place
Apply the mixed colour with gloves on
Time it as the maker says
Rinse, dry and check the shade and the condition
Adjust the shade, developer or time if needed
Record the result

ul: The strand test does **not** check for an allergy. Only the skin test does that.
If the strand is too light, too dark or the hair feels weak, change the plan before you colour the head.

sections.title: Choosing, mixing and applying the colour

head: Goal
Usual approach
rows: Same level, new tone or grey cover
20 volume (or the maker's chart); a shade at the same level as her natural base
One level darker
Low-strength developer, as the maker's chart shows, or a deposit-only colour
One to two levels lighter
20 volume, as the maker advises
Two to three levels lighter
30 volume, as the maker advises; more risk to the hair; a strand test is essential
More than three levels lighter
Lightener (bleach); an instructor's decision; a toner afterwards
Cancelling unwanted tone
Use the opposite colour: ash or blue-based for orange, violet-based for yellow, matt for red
Covering a lot of grey
A shade with some natural tone (neutral), at or just above her natural level; pre-soften or allow the full time as the maker says

blocks.note: These are general choices. Always follow the maker's chart for the shade, the developer and the mixing ratio. Ask your instructor if the plan is not clear.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Mix in a clean plastic or glass bowl with a tint brush, just before use.
Measure the colour and developer in the amounts the maker says (often equal parts, but check). Measure with a measuring bottle or scale, not by eye.
Mix until smooth. Do not store it or add more developer later.
Use the colour and developer from the same maker.

flow: Gown the client with a cape and towel
Put on gloves and an apron
Put barrier cream round the hairline, ears and nape
Place cotton wool or a neck strip at the hairline
Detangle gently; do not scratch the scalp
Divide the hair into four sections: centre parting and ear-to-ear
Clip each section

ul: Do not shampoo the hair before colouring unless the maker says; the scalp's natural oils give a little protection.
Dry or damp hair: follow the maker's instructions.

blocks.p: Work in **thin sub-sections** (thin slices of hair), so that the colour covers every hair. Apply the colour with the brush and, with the hair lifted, cover both sides of each slice.

head: Job
Where you apply first
Why
rows: First-time lighter (virgin hair)
Mid-lengths and ends first, roots last
Heat from the scalp makes roots process faster, so applying at the roots first would make them lighter and hotter than the ends. Leave the roots until later in the processing time.
Regrowth (root) retouch
New growth only, at the roots
The lengths already have colour. Overlapping colour on them can darken them and cause bands and damage. If the maker says to refresh the lengths, do so only for the last few minutes.
Same level or darker (no lift)
Roots and lengths together, as the maker says
There is no lightening, so the scalp heat is less important.
Hair with grey
Cover the grey areas first, then the rest, as the maker advises
Grey hair is resistant and needs the full time.

ul: Keep sections clipped until you need them. Work from the most resistant area to the least.
Saturate the hair fully but do not smother the scalp.
Keep colour off the skin; wipe any drops quickly with damp cotton wool.
Keep the sub-sections thin and the same size.

blocks.note: 'Hot roots' happens when the scalp's heat makes the roots go lighter or warmer than the lengths. This is why the roots go on last when lightening virgin hair.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Process for the **full time the maker says**. Set a timer and note the start time on the record card.
Do not put the client under a dryer or heat unless the maker says. Heat speeds processing and can harm the hair or scalp.
Check the colour at the time the maker says, by wiping a little colour from a strand with a damp piece of cotton wool or a tissue.
Check the client often. Ask whether she feels any itching or burning. **Rinse at once** if she does.

flow: When the time is up, add a little warm water to the colour on the head
Massage gently with your fingertips (emulsify)
Rinse thoroughly with lukewarm water until it runs clear
Shampoo with a colour-care, acid-balanced shampoo
Apply a conditioner or acid-balanced finishing treatment
Rinse; remove stains from the skin
Style as the client wants and check the colour in daylight

ul: **Emulsifying** loosens the colour from the hair and the hairline and stops staining. Do it with gloves on.
An acid-balanced conditioner closes the cuticle, locks in the colour and returns the hair to its normal pH.
Remove stains from the skin with a **skin stain remover**, as the maker says. Do not scrub with a stiff brush, and never use bleach on the skin.

sections.title: Grey, relaxed, natural and coloured hair; colour faults

ul: Grey hair has no pigment, and its cuticle is often tight, so colour takes longer to enter.
Use a shade with some natural tone (neutral) so that the grey does not turn out ash or green.
Give the full processing time, and apply to the grey areas first. Some makers advise pre-softening very resistant grey.
Colour covers grey best at or just above the natural level. A very light shade on a lot of grey can look patchy.
Relaxed hair is porous and fragile. Colour can make it break.
Leave the maker's time between a relaxer and colour (often at least 2 weeks), and do a strand test.
Use a gentler developer and a gentle shade, and keep the colour off the lengths on a retouch.
Advise deep conditioning afterwards.
Detangle gently before you start. Use small sections and **full saturation**, because tight coils make it easy to miss hair.
Natural hair is drier and breaks easily, so use a gentler developer where you can and condition after.
Use a low-tension style afterwards. Heat and colour together can be too much for the hair.
The ends are often more porous than the roots, so they take up more colour and can come out darker.
Use the same shade on the roots and a gentler or deposit-only colour on the faded lengths, as the maker says.
Never overlap on a retouch without a good reason.

head: Fault
Likely causes
Prevention or cure
rows: Ends darker than the roots
Porous ends soaked up more colour
Use a gentler or deposit-only colour on the ends; apply to the ends for less time
Dark bands where the colour overlaps
Colour was pulled through onto already-coloured hair
Apply to new growth only; avoid overlap
Brassy, orange or yellow hair after lightening
Warm underlying pigment showed through
Use a toner or an ash or violet-based shade, as the colour wheel says
Colour fades fast
Harsh clarifying shampoo; very hot water; sun, sea and chlorine
Colour-care products; lukewarm water; cover the hair in the sun
Patchy or uneven colour
Thick sub-sections; missed hair; uneven porosity; uneven timing
Thin sub-sections; full saturation; pre-treat porous areas
Colour too dark
Wrong shade; too many levels darker; colour left too long
Choose from the chart and a strand test; time as the maker says. A clarifying shampoo may lighten a little; ask the instructor.
Colour too light or grey shows
Developer too weak; resistant hair; time too short
Use the right developer and time; strand test first
Stains on the skin
No barrier cream; colour dripped
Barrier cream; emulsify; skin stain remover
Dry, brittle or broken hair
Developer too strong; porous hair; overlap; too long
Gentler products; strand test; deep conditioning; trim
Green tone in lightened hair
Chlorine or minerals acting on lightened hair
Chelating shampoo and a toner; ask your instructor

blocks.note: Sun, sea and swimming pools are part of life in Jamaica, and they fade colour and turn lightened hair brassy or green. Advise clients to rinse with fresh water, wear a cap in the sun, and use colour-care products.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tell the client how to keep the colour looking good, and give the reason for each point.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Wait before the first shampoo, as the maker says
The colour is still settling and the cuticle is still lifted
Use colour-care, sulphate-free, acid-balanced shampoo and conditioner
They are milder and help keep the cuticle smooth, so the colour stays in
Wash with lukewarm water; do not wash every day
Hot water lifts the cuticle and fades colour
Do not use a strong clarifying shampoo often
It strips colour and dries the hair
Cover the hair in strong sun; rinse with fresh water after swimming
Sun, sea and chlorine fade and change colour
Deep condition regularly; use a heat protectant
Colour and heat dry the hair
Book a regrowth retouch when new growth shows (often every 4 to 8 weeks)
The roots grow out in the natural colour
Do not colour or relax over colour yourself at home
Overlap and mixed chemicals damage the hair

flow: Throw away the left-over mixed colour as the maker and Centre say
Bin the cotton wool, neck strips and gloves
Wash, then disinfect and dry bowls, brushes and combs
Put used towels and capes in the closed laundry bin
Wipe up stains on surfaces and floors at once
Close tubes and bottles and store them cool and dry
Wipe the trolley with disinfectant
Wash your hands

blocks.p: Write on the client's **record card** at every visit. It helps the next stylist repeat a good result or avoid a problem, and it shows the correct steps were followed if there is a complaint or a reaction.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, name, contact details
07/11/2026, Keisha Thompson, Spanish Town
Hair and scalp analysis
Natural level 3, 20% grey, medium texture, good elasticity; scalp healthy
Past services
Permanent colour 8 weeks ago; no relaxer
Tests
Skin test clear (48 hours before); strand test done, result good
Shade, developer and mixing amounts
Level 4 natural brown; 20 volume; 1:1 by volume, from the same maker
Application and timing
Regrowth only; 35 minutes; emulsified and rinsed
Aftercare given
Colour-care shampoo; wait 48 hours before washing; retouch in 6 weeks
Problems or reactions
None
Stylist and instructor check
M. Francis (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure: store cards in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, and never discuss a client's hair, health or tests with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can say why gloves, an apron, barrier cream and ventilation are used with colour.
I can give first aid for colour in the eye or on the skin and say when to stop the service.
I can store and handle colour and developer safely and say why mixed colour is never stored.
I can use the level system and say what level 1 and level 10 are.
I can say what tone is, and tell warm, cool and neutral apart.
I can name the primary and secondary colours and use the colour wheel to cancel orange, yellow and red.
I can explain what shows when dark hair is lightened.
I can explain how permanent colour works inside the hair.
I can tell permanent, demi-permanent, semi-permanent and lightener apart.
I can compare developer strengths (10, 20, 30 and 40 volume).
I can do a consultation and find the natural level, grey and condition.
I can do and read a skin test and a strand test.
I can list the contra-indications to colour.
I can choose the shade and developer for a goal.
I can section the hair and apply colour to virgin hair, regrowth and darker colours.
I can process, emulsify, rinse and finish the colour.
I can adapt for grey, relaxed, natural and previously coloured hair.
I can name colour faults, their causes and their cures.
I can give aftercare advice, clean up and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I apply colour to the roots last on virgin hair because heat from the scalp makes them process faster.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: How light or dark a hair colour is, on a scale from 1 (black) to 10 (lightest blonde).
The colour you see: warm, cool or neutral.
Orange, green and violet; each made by mixing two primaries.
Cancel an unwanted tone with the colour opposite it on the wheel.
The natural pigment that gives hair its colour.
The warm pigment uncovered when dark hair is lightened.
The middle layer of the hair, where colour molecules are trapped.
The part of permanent colour that swells the hair and opens the cuticle.
Hydrogen peroxide mixed with colour; lightens pigment and develops the colour.
A name for developer strength, for example 10, 20, 30 or 40 volume.
Colour that needs developer to develop; permanent colour.
How many levels lighter the colour makes the hair.
A product that removes natural pigment to lighten hair by many levels.
A product that adjusts the tone of lightened hair.
Hair that has never had a chemical service.
New growth at the roots in the natural colour.
A small test on the skin to find out whether the client is allergic to the colour.
A test on a small piece of hair to check the result and timing.
A cream on the skin round the hairline to stop staining.
A thin slice of hair used when applying colour.
Cover every hair fully with colour.
Add a little warm water to the colour and massage it before rinsing.
A visible line where colour overlaps or new growth meets coloured hair.
Roots that go lighter or warmer than the lengths because of scalp heat.
Hair that does not take in liquid or colour easily; often grey hair.
The client's record of her hair, tests, shade, developer, timing, advice and any reactions.

c1.title: Covering grey in Montego Bay
c1.text: Mr. Winston Hall, 52, comes to a salon in Montego Bay. About half of his short hair is grey, and the rest is natural level 3. He wants a natural dark brown with no one noticing the grey. He had a skin test 48 hours ago with no reaction. Trainee Kadeem sees that the grey hair is wiry, and Mr. Hall says that his last home colour 'never took' on the grey patches.

c2.title: A golden blonde wish in Kingston
c2.text: Alicia Morgan, 25, has natural level 4 hair that has never been coloured. She shows trainee Dwight a photograph of very light golden blonde hair and wants it in one visit. She has a clear skin test. She says she swims twice a week and washes her hair every day with a strong clarifying shampoo.

c3.title: A retouch in Portmore
c3.text: Sherene Brown, 41, wants a retouch. Eight weeks ago she had a permanent copper colour over level 4 hair, and now 2 cm of dark new growth shows. Her ends have faded and are dry. Trainee Tamara plans to pull the colour through to the ends to refresh them, and to leave it on for the full time on all of the hair. A clear skin test was done 48 hours ago.

c4.title: A messy station at the Centre
c4.text: During a practical session in the Centre's salon in Mandeville, trainee Garfield mixes colour and developer in a metal bowl and without gloves, because 'it is only a quick mix'. He mixes enough for two clients and puts the left-over mix in a plastic bottle for the next day. He skips the barrier cream, and a drop of colour runs down the client's forehead. He has no record of a skin test for the client.

c5.title: Brassy hair after the beach
c5.text: Marsha Reid, 30, lightened her hair to a light brown at a salon in Negril two months ago. She swims in the sea most weekends. Her hair has gone orange and a little brassy, and the ends are dry. She asks trainee Andrene to 'fix it' with a lighter permanent colour.

questions.q: Why is Mr. Hall's grey hair harder to colour than the rest of his hair?
o: It has no pigment, and its cuticle is often tight
It has too much pigment, which blocks the colour
It is very porous, so the colour washes straight out
It grows faster, so the colour is rubbed away
questions.why: Grey hair has lost its pigment, and its cuticle is often tight, so colour enters slowly and may not cover. Give it the full time, apply to the grey areas first, and use a shade with natural tone.

questions.q: Which choice suits Mr. Hall best?
o: A very light shade at level 6, so the grey hardly shows
A natural-toned shade at level 3 or 4, with 20 volume developer
A very strong 40 volume developer, to force open the grey hair
A semi-permanent shade, since it needs no developer at all
questions.why: Covering grey works best with a shade with natural tone at or just above the natural level, with a developer such as 20 volume. A very light shade on half-grey hair looks patchy, 40 volume is too harsh, and semi-permanent colour does not cover grey fully.

questions.q: Mr. Hall's skin test was clear 48 hours ago. What should Kadeem do before colouring the whole head?
o: Skip any other test, since the skin test covers everything
Do a strand test, to check the result and timing
Colour the head, and test a strand at the end
Repeat the skin test on his hairline
questions.why: The skin test checks for allergy only. A strand test checks the shade, the timing and the hair's reaction, so that you can adjust the plan before the whole head.

questions.q: Mr. Hall says his last home colour 'never took' on the grey. What should Kadeem do about timing?
o: Rinse early, as grey hair takes colour faster than other hair
Process for twice the maker's time, to make sure it takes
Add heat from a dryer, to cut the processing time
Give the full time the maker says, and apply to the grey first
questions.why: Grey hair needs the full processing time, and applying to the grey areas first gives it the longest. Doubling the time, or adding heat, risks the scalp and the hair; rinsing early leaves the grey uncovered.

questions.q: What does the golden blonde Alicia wants mean for her natural level 4 hair?
o: It needs only a low-strength developer and a golden shade
It needs lightening by many levels, often with bleach and a toner
It needs a demi-permanent colour, which lifts as far as needed
It needs a darker colour first, to build up a base
questions.why: Level 4 to a very light blonde is about five or six levels of lift. Permanent colour cannot do that, so lightener is needed, with a toner afterwards. It is a harsh, multi-step job that needs an instructor's decision.

questions.q: After Alicia's dark hair is bleached, it looks pale orange-yellow. Why is a toner used next?
o: Bleach leaves warm tones, and the toner cancels them out
Bleach leaves the hair too dark, and the toner lightens it
Bleach leaves the cuticle shut, and the toner opens it
Bleach leaves the hair without any colour, and the toner dyes it permanently
questions.why: Lightening uncovers warm underlying pigments, so bleached dark hair looks orange or yellow. A toner with an opposite tone, such as ash or violet-based, cancels them and gives a cleaner blonde.

questions.q: What is the best way for trainee Dwight to answer Alicia's request for blonde in one visit?
o: Agree, and use the strongest developer to get there in one go
Agree, and apply the colour to her roots first to speed it up
Explain it takes several steps and risks her hair, and offer a gentler plan
Refuse to colour her hair at all, because blonde can never be done
questions.why: Be honest. Going many levels lighter is slow and risky, and a rushed attempt damages the hair. Offer a plan in stages, with a strand test and conditioning between, or a shade closer to her level.

questions.q: Alicia swims twice a week and washes with a strong clarifying shampoo daily. Which aftercare advice is best?
o: Keep using the clarifying shampoo daily, to remove the chlorine
Wash in very hot water, to close the colour in
Use colour-care products, cooler water and a fresh-water rinse
Stop washing her hair for a whole month
questions.why: Strong shampoo, hot water, sun and chlorine all lift the cuticle and fade or change colour. Colour-care products, lukewarm water and protection from chlorine keep colour and hair healthier.

questions.q: What is the problem with Tamara's plan to pull the colour through to the ends for the full time?
o: The ends will turn lighter than the roots because they are older
The ends will refuse to take colour because they are already coloured
The ends will stain Sherene's skin more than the roots would
The porous ends will soak up colour, go darker and be damaged
questions.why: Overlapping on already-coloured hair builds up colour, makes the ends darker than the roots and can cause bands and dryness. A retouch goes on the new growth only; the lengths are refreshed only for the last few minutes if the maker says.

questions.q: Where should Tamara apply the colour first?
o: Only to the new growth at her roots
To the ends first, then the roots
To the whole head at once
To the scalp, so that it soaks up to the roots
questions.why: On a retouch the colour goes on the new growth only. Putting it on the scalp is unsafe, and putting it on the ends first or on the whole head causes overlap and damage.

questions.q: Sherene's copper colour was put on 8 weeks ago. What would a good record card show after this visit?
o: Only the date, since colour is the same each time
The shade, developer, mixing amounts, timing and tests
Just the price paid and her phone number
Only the shade, so the receptionist can order it
questions.why: A full record helps the next stylist repeat a good result or avoid a problem, and shows the correct steps were followed. It includes tests, shade, developer, mixing amounts, timing, aftercare and any reaction.

questions.q: How can Tamara refresh Sherene's dry, faded ends safely?
o: Use a gentler or deposit-only colour on the ends, for a short time
Leave the full-strength mix on the ends for the whole time
Apply a stronger developer to the ends to bring the colour back
Skip the ends and tell her colour cannot be refreshed
questions.why: Faded ends are porous. A gentler, deposit-only colour for a short time, as the maker says, refreshes them without overloading or damaging them.

questions.q: What is wrong with Garfield mixing in a metal bowl?
o: Metal makes the colour too thick to apply smoothly
Metal can react with the chemicals and spoil the result
The bowl is too heavy to hold while he is mixing it
Metal bowls cannot be cleaned properly afterwards
questions.why: Metal can react with colour and developer and change the result. Use a clean plastic or glass bowl and a tint brush.

questions.q: What should Garfield do with the left-over mixed colour?
o: Keep it in the bottle in the fridge for tomorrow
Add a little water and keep it for the next client
Throw it away as the maker and Centre say
Pour it back into the tube to use another day
questions.why: Mixed colour is a live chemical that keeps reacting, so it changes in strength and cannot be stored. Mix only what you need, and throw away what is left.

questions.q: A drop of colour has run down the client's forehead. What is the best action?
o: Leave it, since it will wash off in the shampoo
Rub it hard with a stiff brush straight away
Wipe it with a little bleach on cotton wool
Wipe it at once with damp cotton wool, then use a stain remover
questions.why: Wipe drips as soon as they happen, and remove any stain afterwards with a skin stain remover as the maker says. Scrubbing hard or using bleach harms the skin.

questions.q: The client has no skin test recorded. What should Garfield do?
o: Colour the head and watch for a reaction
Test a strand of hair instead of the skin
Not colour until a skin test has been done and read
Do a skin test now and colour straight away
questions.why: A skin test must be done and read before colour, usually about 48 hours earlier. A strand test does not check for allergy, and testing now does not leave time to see the reaction.

questions.q: Why is a lighter permanent colour the wrong answer for Marsha's orange hair?
o: Colour cannot lift colour already in her hair, and would add damage
Permanent colour only ever makes hair darker, whatever its condition
A lighter colour would turn her hair green at once, as chlorine reacts
Orange hair cannot take any colour at all, however it is applied
questions.why: Colour does not lift colour, and her ends are dry. The right fix is to cancel the orange with a blue-based (ash) toner at her level, with conditioning.

questions.q: Andrene decides on a toner. Why should she do a strand test on Marsha's dry ends first?
o: To check she is not allergic to the toner itself
To check the shade, timing and reaction before the whole head
To make the toner process faster on the dry ends
To lift more of the orange out of the hair first
questions.why: A strand test shows the result, the timing and how the hair takes the product, so that you can adjust the plan before the whole head. Only a skin test checks for allergy, and it does not speed or lift anything.

questions.q: Which product in a permanent colour mix opens the cuticle so colour can enter the hair?
o: The developer, which is hydrogen peroxide
The small colour molecules themselves
The alkali, such as ammonia
The barrier cream round the hairline
questions.why: The alkali swells the hair and lifts the cuticle so that the small colour molecules can enter the cortex. The developer then lightens pigment and joins the colour molecules together.

questions.q: A tube is labelled 20 volume developer. About what percentage of hydrogen peroxide does this mean?
o: About 3%
About 6%
About 9%
About 12%
questions.why: Developer is named by volume or percentage: 10 volume is about 3%, 20 volume about 6%, 30 volume about 9% and 40 volume about 12%. Check the label, because makers' names differ.
